en: I take refuge in you alone, Śambhu—the supreme, the one who stands beyond, the beginningless, the singular who dwells in many secret places, the abode of all, and who resides within all that is moving and unmoving. // 1 //

Having wandered through the wheel of suffering beginning with dwelling in the womb and ending with death, the disciple questioned the Blessed One, the foundation, regarding the ultimate truth. // 2 //
Abhinavagupta speaks of that essence by means of the *Ādhārakārikās*, employing the perspective of the Śiva-scripture, as the Guru addressed him. (3)
By the weight of the majesty of His own power, the Lord has manifested this fourfold body through its divisions as Śakti, Māyā, Prakṛti, and Pṛthvī.
Within that [Śiva], there exists this entire universe— a continuous stream of diverse bodies, instruments, and worlds—
and therein the embodied enjoyer is none other than Śiva himself, who has assumed the state of a bound soul (paśu).
Just as a pure crystal assumes the forms of various colors, so too does the Lord assume the forms of gods, humans, animals, and plants.
Just as the reflection of the moon moves when the water moves and remains still when it is still,
so too does this Great Lord, the Self, move or remain still according to the collection of the body, the senses, and the world.

Just as Rāhu, though invisible, becomes manifest when situated within the lunar orb, so too this Self, although omnipresent, becomes manifest by taking the objects as its support within the mirror of the intellect.
Just as a face shines clearly in a mirror free from dust, so too does this [Self],
whose nature is light, shine within the principle of consciousness made pure by the descent of Śiva’s power.
It is the form of light, complete through resting within its own self as great bliss,
filled with the instruments of will and consciousness, and fully endowed with infinite power.
In that Supreme Reality— which is devoid of all conceptual construction, pure, tranquil, and free from both dissolution and emergence—
the universe, consisting of thirty-six principles, shines forth.

Just as the variegated forms of cities, villages, and so forth appear within the surface of a mirror as something undivided, yet they appear as if divided from one another and also from the mirror itself; (12)

Due to the most stainless and supreme awakening of Bhairava, this world, although devoid of division in that same manner, nevertheless appears as mutually distinct and distinct from that [awakening] as well. (13)
It manifests the state of the principles consisting of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā,
through the differentiated manifestation of the five powers.
The supreme sovereignty of Maheśa, which accomplishes the impossible, is the Goddess Māyā-śakti; she is the veil over the self of Śiva. (15)
Due to the influence of the grasping of Māyā, the conscious person becomes stained and a bound soul (paśu);
he is fettered by the power of Kāla, Kalā, and Niyati, and under the sway of Rāga and Avidyā. // 16 //
I know this very thing now, indeed, with my whole being;
it has been stated that this sixfold sheath, together with Māyā, is the innermost [nature] of the individual soul (aṇu). // 17 //
Like a grain of rice situated within its husk, it remains undifferentiated even when separated;
yet, through the application of the path to Śiva, it attains purity.

Prakṛti consists merely of pleasure, pain, and delusion; furthermore, through the sequence of determination, conceptualization, and self-conceit, it becomes the internal organ—namely, intellect, mind, and ego. (19)

The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are the organs of cognition with respect to sound and the other sense objects; furthermore, speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ are the organs of action. (20)
The object of apprehension for these [five senses] is subtle and devoid of differentiation;
that is the pentad of *tanmātras*: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. (21)
Through the power of association with these [subtle elements], the gross object attains the state of the five elements: ether, wind, fire, water, and earth. (22)
Like the husk enveloping the grain of rice, this creation, preceded by primordial nature (prakṛti), covers consciousness with the state of a body, extending as far as the earth. (23)

The supreme obscuration here is the subtle impurity consisting of the sheaths such as Māyā; the gross [obscuration] is the external form of the body. Indeed, the Self is enveloped by these three coverings.
Due to the conjunction with the darkness of ignorance, one perceives even one's own single nature, the self, through the manifold variety of the grasped and the grasper. // 25 //
Just as juice, molasses, sugar, jaggery, and so forth are nothing but sugarcane juice itself, even so are all the various states of the Supreme Self, Śambhu. 26.

From consciousness, through the inner controller, the vital breath, the cosmic body (Virāj), the physical body, and birth, up to the body of the social order—all these are mere conventional designations; in the ultimate sense, however, they do not exist at all. // 27 //
There is no serpent in the rope, yet it causes terror that culminates in death; indeed, the power of delusion is so great that it cannot be discerned. (28)

In the same way, dharma and adharma, heaven and hell, birth and death, pleasure and pain, and the system of castes and stages of life—though non-existent in the Self—come to be through the power of delusion. (29)
This is that very darkness: this conceit of "self" which occurs with respect to phenomena—even though they are not distinct from the self—by virtue of their appearing as such. (30)
This is darkness upon darkness, this is a great swelling atop the river Ganges:
that there is a sense of self-conceit (*ātmamānitva*) even toward what is not the self, such as the body and the vital breaths. (31)
Through the expansion of the sky of consciousness—consisting of the intellect and the awareness of the body and vital breath—it wonderfully envelops itself, like a spider with its web. (32)
"By means of the yoga of the manifestation of the power of his own consciousness, he should unbind his own self;
thus does Paramaśiva perform this wondrous play of bondage and liberation. (33)
Creation, maintenance, and dissolution, as well as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, shine within that fourth state (turiya); yet even so, it shines forth unenveloped by them.

The waking state is Viśva due to differentiation; the dream state is Taijasa due to the majesty of its luminosity; the deep sleep state is Prājña because it is a mass of consciousness; beyond that is the Fourth (Turya). // 35 //
Just as the expanse of the sky is not soiled by clouds, smoke, or dust,
even so the Supreme Person is untouched by the transformations of *māyā*.
Just as when the space within one jar is pervaded by dust, the others do not become soiled; likewise, these individual souls (jīvas) experience the distinctions of pleasure and pain.
When [the mind] is peaceful, this [Lord] appears as if peaceful; when it is joyful, he appears joyful; and when it is deluded, he appears deluded.
Yet, while the collection of principles exists, the Blessed One is not actually so in the ultimate sense.
Having previously refuted that appearance of such a form even in what is not the self, the Supreme Self shatters the delusion of the nature of a non-self within the self. (39)
Thus, for the supreme yogin who has achieved his purpose by completely severing the very root of the pair of delusions, there never arises any further perception of tasks to be performed. (40)

Earth, primordial nature (prakṛti), and illusion (māyā)—this triad has fallen into the state of being an object of cognition; yet, through the power of the contemplation of non-duality, it indeed remains as nothing but pure existence (sanmātra). // 41 //
Just as gold is seen when the distinctions of girdles, earrings, and bracelets are abandoned, so too,
when distinctions are abandoned, everything appears as pure existence alone.
That Brahman is supreme, pure, tranquil, non-dual in nature, equal, and all-encompassing;
it is immortal and true, and it rests within the radiant Power (Śakti). // 43 //
It is desired, it is known, and it is accomplished in the form of light;
yet, even so, that which is untouched [by conceptualization] becomes like a flower in the sky.
By means of the union with the trident of power, the God of gods emits even the entire universe into the Supreme Lord, the ultimate reality named Śiva.
Furthermore, by means of the sequence of the expansion of the five powers, those three diverse limbs are also created externally through the attainment of an external self-nature. (46)
Thus, by means of the yoga of play, the Lord moves the machine of the wheel of powers;
I myself am the pure form, established in the station of the leader of the great wheel of powers. // 47 //
The entire universe shines within me alone, like jars and other objects in a stainless mirror; everything emanates from me, like the manifold variety of a dream from one who sleeps.
I alone am the universal form; like the body whose nature consists of hands, feet, and so forth, I alone manifest within all things, like luminous light. (49)
Though devoid of body and senses, I alone am the seer, the hearer, and the smeller; and though I am a non-doer, I myself compose the various systems of tenets, scriptures, and reasonings. (50)
Thus, when the conceptualization of duality has dissolved and the delusive *māyā* has been transcended, one should become absorbed in Brahman, like water in water or milk in milk. (51)

Thus, when the entire collection of principles has been transformed into the nature of Śiva through meditation, what grief and what delusion can there be for one who perceives everything as Brahman? (52)
Wholesome and unwholesome karmic fruit arises solely from association with false knowledge;
for the fault of association is as treacherous as the company of a thief to one who is not a thief. (53)
Those fools who here worship ignorance, which is created by worldly convention, go to birth and death, bound by the bolts of merit and demerit. (54)
Even karma, consisting of merit and demerit, accumulated during the time of ignorance, perishes through the power of the light of higher knowledge, just like long-gathered cotton. // 55 //
Since even that which has been performed does not lead to fruit once knowledge is attained, how could there be further birth for him?
Having transcended the bond of birth, he shines as the sun of Śiva by means of his own rays.

Just as a seed freed from its husk, chaff, and awn produces a sprout, so too the Self, when liberated from the impurities of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārma* bonds, does not produce the sprout of existence. 57.
One who knows the Self fears nothing whatsoever, for everything is his own true nature;
nor does he grieve, because in the ultimate sense there is no destruction.

Since the collection of jewels of ultimate reality has grown within the treasury of the exceedingly profound heart, what misfortune could there be, and for whom, in the state of being the Great Lord? (59)
Liberation has no abode whatsoever, nor does it involve going anywhere else;
liberation is simply the bursting of the knot of ignorance and the manifestation of one's own innate power.
With the knot of ignorance severed, doubt gone, and delusion dispelled;
with merit and demerit exhausted, he is liberated even while joined to a physical body. (61)
Just as a seed scorched by fire becomes incapable of sprouting,
so too karma burnt by the fire of knowledge does not lead to rebirth.

For consciousness, being limited by the intellect, is contracted through the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) of a future body appropriate for its karma; thus it appears in that manner upon the destruction of this present body.

If, moreover, there were a stainless awakening, consisting of a cognizer and agent that has transcended all things, pervasive, of the nature of light that neither sets nor rises, and whose volition is true; // 64 //
The Lord is devoid of spatial and temporal divisions, eternal, immutable, perfectly full, and the sole agent in the creation, dissolution, and emergence of the vast multitude of powers. // 65 //
One should realize oneself as Śiva, the supreme creator of the laws of creation and so forth;
how then could one be a transmigrating being? For one who is all-pervading, whence or whither could there be any wandering?
Thus, it is established even by reason that the action of a man of knowledge is not fruitful;
for in this world, no fruit arises from the firm conviction, "This is not mine, but his."
Thus, having awakened from all conceptual constructions through the wind of meditative cultivation,
one becomes composed of light by offering them into the blazing light of the self.
Eating whatever it may be, clothed in whatever manner, peaceful, and dwelling wherever one may be, he whose self is the soul of all beings is liberated.
Even if one performs hundreds of thousands of horse-sacrifices or commits hundreds of thousands of killings of Brahmins,
the knower of the ultimate truth remains stainless, untouched by either merit or sin.
Free from intoxication, joy, anger, passion, despondency, fear, greed, and delusion,
devoid of praise and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he should wander like one who is dull-witted, his mind beyond the reach of debate.
This category beginning with intoxication and exhilaration arises from the delusion of differentiation;
how, then, could it possibly touch the awakening to the non-dual Self? (72)
There is nothing whatsoever separate from Him that is to be praised or offered;
yet He may be pleased by hymns and the like, being liberated and devoid of salutation, *namas*, or the *vaṣaṭ* call. (73)
His own body, or another body, or even a jar and so forth, becomes his temple—a structure filled with the thirty-six principles and complete with windows formed by its various limbs. (74)
And there he remains, worshipping with substances purified by self-reflection the deity Śiva as the Supreme Self-Mahābhairava, together with his own Śakti.

For one who offers the great mass of seeds consisting of the various conceptualizations of the internal and external, the oblation occurs effortlessly in the intensely blazing fire of pure consciousness. // 76 //
Furthermore, this Blessed One creates various forms through a meditation that never sets;
for that very meditation is the state in which the true nature [of things] is inscribed by his volition.

That which revolves the entire series of worlds, the conceptualization of the sequence of principles, and the group of sense organs within internal consciousness—that is declared to be his recitation (japa). 78.

Everything that one sees with the vision of the pledge (samaya) and whatever consciousness one perceives is dedicated to the cremation ground of the universe, adorned with the conceptualization of a body and a khaṭvāṅga staff. (79)
He holds in his own hand a skull-bowl, the vessel of knowledge, filled with the nectar of universal flavor;
that he partakes of this is his vow, which is both very difficult to attain and easily attained. 80.
Thus, having realized that which is devoid of birth and destruction, known as the Supreme Lord of Ultimate Reality,
one remains at ease as one pleases, having accomplished all that was to be done, due to the manifestation of the state of being the perceiver.
He who knows the all-pervading one thus described—the self of all, from whom diversity has been shaken off, and who is incomparable supreme bliss—becomes absorbed in that very essence. (82)

Whether at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste, even if his memory has failed, one who casts off the body is liberated simultaneously with the arising of knowledge and, with sorrow destroyed, attains absolute isolation.
Visiting sacred fords leads to merit; going to the home of a dog-cooker at the time of death leads to hell.
But when there is no contact with the stain of either merit or demerit, what is the use of that?

Just as the husk and the outer shell are thoroughly separated from the grain of rice, and once cast away between the husk and the grain, they no longer possess the same nature or identity as that grain; so it is here. (85)
In the same way, consciousness here, when separated from the veil of the sheaths (kañcuka) through purification, remains as one whose self is liberated, devoid of contact with them. // 86 //

Just as a gem, though soiled, possesses a state of stainlessness fashioned by the most skillful artisan within its casing, yet when separated from that casing, it is transparent in its ultimate nature; so too is the mind. (87)

Thus, for one who possesses the stainless state of the teaching of a true guru, the experience of the subtle body's limitation appears as the form of Śiva— though already liberated— as if it were devoid of any further limiting adjuncts.

Even through unwavering faith based on the authority of the scriptures and other sources, he who has attained identification with that [object of faith] first experiences heaven, hell, and the human state. (89)
But the final moment, while sustaining a meritorious or sinful state within that [stream], becomes a cooperative cause for the deluded; however, once motion has occurred, it is no longer a cause.
Even those animals, birds, reptiles, and so forth, who know their own destiny as being of that very nature, go to that state because they have been conditioned by ancient impressions of awakening.
This person, situated within the interval of the body, consists of heaven and consists of hell;
upon the destruction of that [body], he attains union with another body according to his own fitness.
Thus, at the moment of realization, in whatever manner one's own self appears to him once and for all, it remains exactly so even after the fall of the body; it does not become otherwise.

The loss of the collection of instruments, the destruction of memory, the turbidity of breath, the cutting [of the channels], and specific pains in the vital points—this is the experience born from the refinement of the body. // 94 //

How could that [knowledge] not exist when there is the conjunction with a body? Therefore, even when there is the conjunction with delusion, at the moment of death, the knower does not fall away from the ultimate reality of his own self.
When one suddenly attains this path of ultimate reality from the mouth of the Guru due to an extremely intense descent of power (śaktipāta), then and there one becomes Śiva, free from all obstacles.
For one who ascends by means of the sequence of steps toward the form that transcends all,
there occurs at the final limit, upon attaining the ascent to the supreme reality, the state of being identical with Śiva.

However, for one who has not yet reached the stream consisting of ultimate reality and rests only in the middle state, death may sometimes occur even though his mind is eager to attain that state. (98)
One who has fallen from yoga is described in the scripture as a lord of worlds of variegated enjoyments;
by virtue of finding rest there, he becomes Śiva in another birth. (99)

For by practicing this path of ultimate reality, even if one does not attain yoga itself, one partakes in the enjoyments of the celestial realms and rejoices with a joyful mind for a very long time. (100)
Just as a sovereign emperor is honored by all people within his realm, so too is one who has fallen from yoga honored at all times by all the gods throughout the worlds. (101)
After a long time, having again attained human birth and practiced yoga, one attains the divine nectar from which one does not return again. // 102 //
Therefore, thinking that "whoever is devoted to this true path attains the state of Śiva," one should strive for the ultimate reality by whatever means possible. 103.
For one who meditates upon this supreme Brahman according to the summary proclaimed by Abhinavagupta, the state of Śiva—the penetration into one's own heart—attains him very soon indeed. (104)
This extremely profound essence of the treatise, consisting of one hundred Āryā verses, has been condensed by me, Abhinavagupta, who is illumined by the remembrance of the feet of Śiva. 105.
